# Appendix I — Decision Catalog

This catalog lists the recurring decisions from the Decision & Trade-off callouts of each chapter, with the options compared. The section each entry links to gives the conditions for choosing an option and the consequences.

## I.1 Chapter 1: Architecture Requirements

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How much structure a functional requirement needs before design starts. | Capability and outcome statement only; Use case with explicit exception paths; Executable acceptance specification | 1.1 |
| How to resolve competing quality attributes before design commits to one. | Optimize each attribute against its own target; Rank scenarios and allocate a shared budget; Adopt platform defaults and revisit after launch | 1.2 |
| What to do when a constraint blocks the better design. | Design within the constraint; Time-boxed exception with a named risk owner; Escalate to change the constraint | 1.3 |
| A quality goal is often stated as an adjective. Decide how to treat it before it drives a design. | Measurable scenario with target; Assumption with owner and expiry; Constraint with source | 1.4 |
| How to keep requirement links alive for the life of the solution. | Identifier links in a requirements tool; Links between records in version control; Narrative references only | 1.5 |

: Decisions from Chapter 1

## I.2 Chapter 2: Architecture Principles

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A principle costs effort to write and maintain, so decide how much structure each one earns. | Full anatomy for every principle; Full anatomy for binding principles, one-line guidance elsewhere; No published principles, rely on review | 2.1 |
| Not every justified change has a revenue indicator; decide what evidence a business case must carry. | Outcome with baseline and target; Named risk reduction with a risk owner; Bounded experiment with a stop rule | 2.2 |
| Decide how much structural complexity the next two years of change justify. | Modular monolith with enforced boundaries; Coarse services per capability; Extract a service later, behind an existing module boundary | 2.3 |
| Boundaries decay unless something enforces them; choose the enforcement that matches the team’s size. | Convention and review; Automated dependency checks in CI; Separate deployables per module | 2.4 |
| Ownership can be enforced at different strengths; choose one deliberately. | One owning service per fact, writes only through its API; Shared schema with per-table ownership and grants; Domain-owned data product with a published contract | 2.5 |
| The interaction style drives most of the operational cost; decide it explicitly. | Synchronous request and response; Asynchronous message or event; Batch file exchange | 2.6 |
| Where authorization lives determines how much duplication the team carries. | Authorize in each owning service; Central policy engine called by services; Authorize at the gateway only | 2.7 |
| How a system fails is a design decision with a customer-visible consequence. | Fail fast and reject; Degrade with a fallback; Queue the work and replay | 2.8 |
| Scaling options differ in cost and reversibility; decide with measurement, not preference. | Scale up; Scale out; Reduce work: cache or defer | 2.9 |
| Instrumentation scope is a cost and privacy decision as well as a technical one. | Journey-based instrumentation; Platform default for every service; Vendor agent with automatic tracing | 2.10 |
| Isolation costs code now and saves migration later; pick the level the risk justifies. | Domain port with an adapter; Shared client library owned by the platform; Call the SDK directly from domain code | 2.11 |
| Standardization trades local fit for consistency; choose the balance deliberately. | Central platform, mandated; Paved road with a documented exception route; Team autonomy with published guidance | 2.12 |
| Every decision can be escalated; the choice is where review stops adding value. | Team decides and records briefly; Consult affected owners, then decide; Focused review with a risk owner | 2.13 |
| Privacy controls restrict what the system can do; choose the strength deliberately. | Collect only the fields the journey needs; Pseudonymize and separate identifiers; Retain full data under strict access control | 2.14 |
| Evidence costs effort to produce and keep; decide what must be retained. | Record every decision with full evidence; Record significant decisions, sample the rest; Rely on tickets and chat history | 2.15 |
| When principles conflict, decide how the conflict will be resolved and recorded. | Revise the principle; Time-bound exception; Bounded design compromise | 2.16 |

: Decisions from Chapter 2

## I.3 Chapter 3: Architecture Decisions

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Not every choice needs the same record. Decide the record format before writing it. | ADR; RFC then ADR; Lightweight decision log; Team standard or code review note | 3.1 |
| How to treat a platform mandate set by contract or regulation. | Record the mandate as a constraint; choose the mechanism in an ADR; Record the mandate itself as the decision; Escalate the mandate for renegotiation before deciding | 3.2 |
| Match the depth of the evaluation to the cost of being wrong. | Whiteboard comparison against named criteria; Qualitative matrix with a sensitivity check; Time-boxed spike or benchmark; Formal scenario-based evaluation (ATAM, 18.3.1) | 3.3 |
| When an accepted decision stops holding, choose how to change the record. | Supersede with a new ADR; Add an addendum to the accepted ADR; Amend while the record is still Proposed; Deprecate without a replacement | 3.4 |
| Decide how much traceability to maintain before the first review asks for it. | ADR references only: requirement and interface; Full chain per significant decision; Automated links from code, tests and contracts | 3.5 |

: Decisions from Chapter 3

## I.4 Chapter 4: Architecture Governance

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Choose how authority is distributed before deciding who sits on the council. | Central architecture board; Federated domain authority; Tiered model with published classes | 4.1 |
| Choose how accountability attaches to each decision class. | Single accountable owner; Consensus among stakeholders; Delegated authority with escalation triggers | 4.2 |
| Choose how hard a guardrail should push back. | Blocking gate; Advisory warning; Scheduled drift audit | 4.3 |
| Choose the lightest review mechanism that controls the risk of the change. | Automated guardrail; Peer or architecture review; Architecture council or exception | 4.4 |
| Choose the response when a control cannot be met. | Deny and require redesign; Time-boxed exception with compensating controls; Change the policy | 4.5 |
| Choose how much repository tooling the organization can sustain. | Documents beside the code; Central registry with stable IDs; Graph or CMDB tooling | 4.6 |
| Choose how a fitness function acts on its result. | Blocking gate; Advisory report; Scheduled experiment | 4.7 |
| Choose what the governance report measures. | Meeting volume and attendance; Cycle time and exception age; Escaped risk and verified conditions | 4.8 |
| Choose how much evidence collection to automate. | Manual collection before each audit; Automate evidence for key controls; Continuous compliance for all mapped controls | 4.9 |
| How should a capability needed by several teams be provided? | Each team builds its own; Shared code with inner-source contribution; Platform team offering X-as-a-service; Temporary enabling team | 4.10 |

: Decisions from Chapter 4

## I.5 Chapter 5: Data Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Decide how a principle will be enforced before publishing it. | Automated gate (contract test, policy-as-code, constraint); Manual review with named approver; Exception register with expiry | 5.1 |
| Choose how consumers reach a domain's data before choosing a platform product. | Published API or event from the owner; Governed data product in the platform; Direct read of the owner's tables | 5.2 |
| Choose how a consumer will obtain another domain's data. | Synchronous call to the owner; Event-fed local replica; Governed data product | 5.3 |
| Choose the failure behavior of a critical write path before choosing the datastore. | Refuse or queue the write (favor consistency); Accept the write locally (favor availability); Degrade to read-only | 5.4 |

## I.6 Chapter 6: Integration Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Choose how the caller learns the outcome of a request. | Synchronous response within a deadline; Accepted with a status resource; Notification plus reconciliation | 6.1 |
| Choose how a breaking change will be delivered. | Compatible evolution (expand and contract); New major version running in parallel; New event type or resource | 6.2 |
| Choose where duplicate protection lives. | Consumer inbox with a unique constraint; Provider or remote idempotency key; Status query before retry | 6.3 |
| When the outcome of a remote call is unknown, decide how the workflow recovers. | Blind retry; Status query then reconcile; Fail and compensate | 6.4 |
| Choose where authorization is enforced on an integration. | At the gateway only; In the owning service; Gateway plus service | 6.5 |
| Choose what carries an interface. | Direct contract between owning services; Enterprise bus or iPaaS; Workflow orchestrator; Dedicated adapter service | 6.6 |

: Decisions from Chapter 6

## I.7 Chapter 7: Application Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Decide when a module becomes a service. | Keep the module in the monolith; Extract one service behind its port; Extract several services at once | 7.1 |
| Choose where transaction coordination and validation live. | Application layer handler; Domain aggregate method; Adapter or controller | 7.2 |
| Choose how the application will serve reads before adding a projection or cache. | Direct query of the source; CQRS projection; Shared cache | 7.3 |
| Choose how a dependency failure is isolated. | Bulkhead per dependency; Queue with bounded limits; Asynchronous step with pending state | 7.4 |
| Choose how code is shared between services. | Versioned package in a registry; Module inside a monorepo; Deliberate duplication | 7.5 |
| Choose how clients obtain data shaped for their experience. | One general-purpose API; One BFF per experience; Schema-based aggregation layer | 7.6 |
| Choose how tenant data is separated in the store. | Shared tables with a tenant key and row-level policies; Separate schema or database per tenant on shared servers; Dedicated data stack per tenant or stamp | 7.7 |

## I.8 Chapter 8: Infrastructure and Cloud Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Choose the foundation before choosing products. | New account or subscription in the landing zone; Shared subscription with policy and tagging; Separate landing zone or tenant | 8.1 |
| Choose how recovery will be proven. | Restore drill from backup; Failover exercise to a second region; Tabletop with the business and suppliers | 8.2 |
| Choose how capacity is bought before comparing unit prices. | On-demand, autoscaled; Reserved or committed use against a measured baseline; Provision for the peak and shed or queue the excess | 8.3 |
| Choose the platform operating model. | Self-service golden path; Central platform team with exceptions; Embedded platform engineers per team | 8.4 |
| Choose how many frameworks to apply. | One primary framework per workload; One framework plus provider lenses; Several frameworks in parallel | 8.5 |
| Choose the connectivity and exposure model before selecting network products. | Public ingress with WAF and CDN; Private endpoint, private link or peering; Hybrid VPN or dedicated interconnect; Internal segmentation with service identity | 8.6 |
| Where should service-to-service traffic policy be enforced? | Application libraries; Network policies and a gateway; Service mesh | 8.7 |
| How much intelligence should run at the site? | Thin devices, central processing; Local rules and buffering at a gateway; Full local application and inference | 8.8 |

: Decisions from Chapter 8

## I.9 Chapter 9: Platform Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| What scope should the first platform have? | Thinnest viable platform: conventions, templates and provider services; Curated provider services with guardrails and self-service; Full internal developer platform | 9.1 |
| Should the use of a platform capability be mandatory? | Voluntary, with measured adoption; Mandatory outcome, any compliant implementation; Mandatory capability | 9.2 |
| Who operates a workload that runs on the platform? | The workload team builds and runs it on platform capabilities; Platform operates the runtime; the workload team operates the application; A central operations team operates both | 9.3 |
| How should a golden path deliver its standards to the components it creates? | One-time scaffolding template; Versioned shared modules referenced by components; Platform-managed abstraction | 9.4 |
| What abstraction level should a platform capability expose? | Provider resources with guardrails; Composed building blocks; Application-level abstraction | 9.5 |
| How should workloads share the platform? | Namespaces in a shared runtime; Dedicated runtime per team or domain; Dedicated account or subscription per regulated scope | 9.6 |
| Where should a platform control be enforced? | In the template, as a default; In the pipeline, as a gate; At admission or at runtime | 9.7 |
| How should platform upgrades reach tenants? | Platform-wide upgrade in a maintenance window; Progressive rollout by tenant ring; Tenant-scheduled upgrade within a support window | 9.8 |
| Which evidence should decide the platform's continued funding? | Adoption and experience measures; Delivery and outcome measures against baselines; Cost avoided versus the duplicated alternative | 9.9 |
| How should platform costs reach the consuming teams? | Central funding; Showback; Chargeback | 9.10 |
| How should a platform capability be sourced? | Build in-house; Buy a product or managed platform; Compose provider and open-source parts | 9.11 |
| Who should review the platform's design and operation? | The platform team itself; The architecture review with consuming teams; An external or independent review | 9.12 |

: Decisions from Chapter 9

## I.10 Chapter 10: Security Architecture

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How much threat-modeling depth does this change justify? | Lightweight abuse-path review; STRIDE workshop on the changed flow; Full attack-tree or abuse-case study | 10.1 |
| Which identity model fits this population? | Corporate workforce IdP; CIAM platform; Workload identity federation | 10.2 |
| Where should resource-level authorization live? | Coarse checks at the gateway only; Central policy decision point, enforced in each service; Authorization logic in the owning service | 10.3 |
| Where should keys live? | Provider KMS; Managed HSM; Self-managed key server | 10.4 |
| Which ASVS level should this application target? | L1; L2; L3 | 10.5 |
| How should this vulnerability be handled? | Patch or upgrade; Mitigate with a compensating control; Accept with an exception | 10.6 |
| How should audit evidence be stored? | Standard log platform with retention; Append-only or WORM store; Cryptographic chaining or signing | 10.7 |
| Which assurance route fits this supplier? | SOC 2 Type II; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certificate; PCI DSS AoC | 10.8 |
| How should residency be satisfied? | Regional deployment; Transfer mechanism; In-region keys and access | 10.9 |

## I.11 Chapter 11: Observability, Reliability and SRE

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sampling decides which telemetry is thrown away, and the default discards what an incident needs most. | Head-based sampling in the SDK; Tail-based sampling at the collector; Keep everything on critical journeys, sample elsewhere | 11.1 |
| What should page a person? Page on symptoms that threaten the SLO; route cause-level signals to dashboards and tickets. | Multi-window burn-rate alerts on SLOs; Component threshold alerts (CPU, queue depth, error count); Synthetic probes of critical journeys | 11.2 |
| How much response structure to invoke on a given day decides both speed and overhead. The role split usually starts at SEV2; what matters is that the trigger is written down. | Single responder, escalation on request; Named incident commander and role split at declaration; A standing operations team owns every incident | 11.3 |
| How to meet a known peak, such as a seasonal sale or a migration cut-over. | Provision headroom for the peak; Autoscale on leading indicators; Shed and degrade deliberately | 11.4 |
| How far to take business instrumentation, given that each step adds both detection and cost. | Operational metrics only; Milestone counters and ages; Milestones reconciled against authoritative records | 11.5 |

: Decisions from Chapter 11

## I.12 Chapter 12: Deployment and Operations

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How much environment separation the delivery path needs depends on the risk of the change and on how faithfully a lower environment can represent production. | Ephemeral previews plus one production-like environment; Development, test, staging and production; Production plus a shared pre-production; Blue-green production pair | 12.1 |
| How a change should be exposed depends on whether it needs reversibility, selective reach, or both. | Release flag; Canary cohort by traffic; Deploy-time configuration; No switch; deploy off-peak | 12.2 |
| The strength of the readiness gate should match the cost of being wrong in the first week of operation. | Review with a rehearsed critical failure; Evidence review without rehearsal; Progressive exposure with automatic rollback; No formal gate; rely on rollback | 12.3 |
| The right approval model is the lightest one whose evidence an auditor or an incident review would accept. | Automated, policy-based approval; Peer review with required checks; Delegated, risk-based authority; Change advisory board | 12.4 |
| The production access model trades speed during an incident against the standing exposure it creates. | Just-in-time elevation with approval and expiry; Standing named accounts with session recording; Two-person break-glass | 12.5 |

: Decisions from Chapter 12

## I.13 Chapter 13: Architecture Documentation

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The size of the view set is a decision with a cost on both sides: too few views leave concerns unaddressed, and too many make staleness likely. | Minimum set: context, container and one dynamic view per critical flow; Risk-driven set: minimum plus deployment, data ownership and trust-boundary views where those risks exist; Full catalog of every element and view | 13.1 |
| How much dynamic behavior to model is a scope decision: each branch is cheap to draw and expensive to keep current. | One sequence per critical flow, success path only; Sequence with failure branches plus a data-flow view; Executable interaction model or formal state machine | 13.2 |
| Where the description lives decides who can keep it current and how. | Wiki or shared documents; Docs as code beside the services; Modeling tool with a shared repository | 13.3 |

: Decisions from Chapter 13

## I.14 Chapter 14: Architecture Evaluation

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The weight of an evaluation should follow the cost of being wrong, not the size of the project. Escalate when a review uncovers an unbounded risk or a disputed trade-off; record the chosen weight in the review record (4.4). | Lightweight review: checklist and a peer architect; Scenario-based workshop on the top scenarios; Full ATAM, with CBAM where options differ in cost | 14.1 |
| Who evaluates trades independence against context and cost. | Self-assessment by the design team; Peer evaluators from another team; External evaluation team | 14.2 |
| How evaluation continues after a review trades effort against how quickly a broken assumption is noticed. | Point-in-time evaluation, repeated at major milestones; Evaluation plus monitored triggers and fitness functions; Scheduled periodic re-evaluation, for example yearly | 14.3 |

: Decisions from Chapter 14

## I.15 Chapter 15: Testing and Quality Verification

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The portfolio shape should follow where the architecture’s risk sits, not a fixed picture. | Pyramid: most tests at unit level; Trophy or honeycomb: emphasis on integration and contract tests; Heavy end-to-end suite, as a transitional state | 15.1 |
| Environment strategy trades feedback speed against fidelity, and the right answer differs by test type. | Long-lived shared test environment; Ephemeral environment per change from infrastructure as code; Ephemeral environments plus a production-like environment for performance and recovery | 15.2 |
| Where a quality attribute is tested trades realism against risk to users and data. | Pre-production only, in a production-like environment; Production with controls: canary, feature flags and bounded fault injection; Pre-production for gates and production for confirmation | 15.3 |
| How much test evidence to keep trades audit readiness against storage and effort. | Pipeline logs only, kept for a short period; Structured results per release, linked to scenarios and requirements; Immutable, signed evidence retained as regulation requires | 15.4 |

: Decisions from Chapter 15

## I.16 Chapter 16: Architecture Evolution and Economics

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How should a legacy capability be modernized? | Rehost or replatform the whole capability; Strangler Fig, slice by slice; Rebuild and replace in one release | 16.1 |
| How should a capability be sourced? | Build; Buy a product (licensed or SaaS); Managed platform service | 16.2 |
| How should the roadmap be sequenced? | Capability-by-capability, highest value first; Dependency-first, shared platform early; Risk-first, fragile assets early | 16.3 |

## I.17 Chapter 17: Software Engineering and Architecture Artifacts

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How much design documentation should precede implementation? | Tests and a short design note; ADRs plus updated views and contracts; Full chain: PRD, HLD, ADRs, ICD, LLD, test strategy, runbook | 17.1 |
| How should requirements artifacts be maintained? | One combined requirements document; Separate PRD and SRS with linked identifiers; Requirements in the backlog with scenarios in the architecture repository | 17.2 |

| Where should the interface contract live? | ICD owned by the producer; ICD co-owned with a consumer-driven contract; ICD owned by an integration or platform team | 17.4 |
| How should artifact status and location be managed? | Artifacts in the code repository, reviewed with the change; A document management system with a catalog; A wiki with a maintained index and owners | 17.5 |

| Decision | Options compared | Section |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How much framework should a program adopt? | Lightweight set: quality scenarios, C4, ADRs, tests; Solution set plus arc42 and a review method; Enterprise framework (TOGAF ADM, ArchiMate) on top | 18.1 |
